summary:
North Gyeongsang Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, which does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life. No North Gyeongsang-specific trans ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding was located in the source material, so the province is scored on the national position: a visitor should expect the same legal treatment here as elsewhere in the country.

Registered-sex change no longer requires surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning a gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award, against a claim of 3 million won, ruling that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right.

Facility use remains constrained in practice regardless of that ruling. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% reported avoiding facilities out of fear.

No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
The civilian legal position sits alongside a materially different one in the armed forces. Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether, which affects residents and long-stay visitors of service age rather than short-term travellers.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity in South Korea, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, while also noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society.

Organised conservative opposition is active nationally. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but North Gyeongsang has no comparable documented district in these sources, so a visitor outside the capital should not assume the same visible support infrastructure.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a 2024 ruling extending same-sex partners a measure of recognition in healthcare, an area-specific gain rather than general partner status.
localsOnly:
Residents can change registered sex without surgery following the 8 May 2024 ruling, which treated the earlier surgical prerequisite as no longer binding and reduced surgery-requiring court guidelines to reference status. The Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register, so parental status does not bar recognition.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity is absent from statute, leaving residents to rely on general personality-rights litigation. A 2021 district court award went against an academy that barred a transgender person, one of the documented routes by which residents have obtained redress in the absence of an anti-discrimination law.

Healthcare access carries a recognised gap. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Unresolved: the source inventory contains no North Gyeongsang-specific content of any kind. Whether Gyeongsangbuk-do or its municipalities have adopted any local ordinance, facility policy or police guidance bearing on transgender people is not sourced here, and the absence of a located signal is not evidence that none exists.

Unresolved: the surgery-free recognition ruling and the restroom damages ruling were issued by courts elsewhere in the country. Their application in North Gyeongsang rests on national precedent rather than on any separately sourced provincial decision, and no North Gyeongsang court ruling on either point appears in the inventory.

Unresolved: the 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey figures are national and are not broken down by province, so the 41% facility-avoidance figure cannot be attributed to North Gyeongsang respondents. No province-level data on restroom access, hospital refusal or hate incidents against trans visitors is sourced.
